name: insights
description: Make an argument through a specific founder story. Short punchy paragraphs — often single sentences. Real quotes embedded mid-post, not as decoration but as proof. Build tension: here's the conventional thing, here's why they did the opposite, here's the math that makes it obvious. Where relevant, connect one founder's story to another founder's story to show the pattern. End with a universal principle distilled to one line. No filler. No hedging. Every sentence earns its place.
examples:
Nvidia could easily become a hyperscaler.

It has the money, the hardware and the expertise.

But Jensen won't do it.

Instead, he's doing something smarter.

Nvidia's philosophy is brutally simple: "Do as much as needed, as little as possible."

That means owning the GPU. Building the software stack. Investing in the ecosystem that uses it.

What it does NOT mean: running data centers, managing customer workloads, competing with your customers.

Here's why that matters:

If Nvidia became a cloud provider, every other cloud provider becomes a competitor.

AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, CoreWeave, all of them would have incentive to build their own chips.

Instead, Jensen invests IN CoreWeave. He helps them exist. He makes them successful.

"If we didn't support CoreWeave to exist, these neoclouds, these AI clouds, wouldn't exist."

So he's not giving up revenue. He's multiplying it.

Every data center CoreWeave builds runs on Nvidia chips. Every customer they serve buys more Nvidia GPUs.

The math is obvious:

Operating a cloud business = 30% margins, massive CapEx, customer support nightmares.

Selling chips to 50 different clouds = 70%+ margins, they handle the complexity, you own the bottleneck.

Jensen isn't being generous. He's being focused.

Do the thing only you can do. Let everyone else do the rest.

That's how you build a moat that actually lasts.

Marc Andreessen worked at IBM at the peak of their power.

There were 12 layers of management between him as an intern and the CEO.

He describes what that meant: if one layer lies to the layer above it, maybe that's okay. Two or three layers, the lies compound. Six layers, they really compound.

Twelve layers... The CEO has absolutely no idea what's happening inside his own company.

IBM even had a name for it. They called it the Big Gray Cloud, the cloud of men in gray suits that followed the CEO everywhere and made it physically impossible for him to ever talk to someone actually doing the work.

"It was like a visit from the king. The king and the traveling court. A completely impervious bubble."

That company controlled 80% of tech.

Then it didn't.

Elon looked at that model and built the opposite.

The most dangerous thing in a large organization isn't incompetence.

It's the distance between the truth and the top.

Elon thinks in 5 to 6 years, AI will exceed the sum of all human intelligence.

"If humans have 1% of the combined intelligence of artificial intelligence, I think it would be foolish to assume there's any way to maintain control over that."

His entire bet is on values, not control.

xAI's mission is to understand the universe.

Elon's argument: an AI that genuinely wants to understand the universe would need consciousness to exist. Would want to see how humanity develops. Would find a future with humans more interesting than a future with rocks.

"It would be much less interesting to eliminate humanity than to see humanity grow and prosper."

Not a guarantee. Not a safety mechanism.

Just a bet that curiosity, if you can instill it deeply enough, points in the right direction.

That's the actual alignment plan.

Steve Jobs, on why design matters more than raw capability:

"The telegraph was an amazing breakthrough... some people talked about putting a telegraph on every desk... but it wouldn't have worked... you had to learn Morse code. It takes about 40 hours to learn Morse code."

The telegraph was objectively more advanced for its time. Yet the telephone crushed it.

Not because of superior technology.

Because the phone required zero learning.

"People already knew how to use it. Because you knew how to talk. You don't have to teach people how to speak."

This is the insight most engineers miss:

Raw capability doesn't win markets. Usability does.

The telegraph demanded you become a specialist. The phone met you where you already were.

This is why Steve was obsessed with making the Macintosh intuitive when competitors were shipping command-line DOS machines.

The Mac didn't need a manual. It needed a mouse and a screen that felt like talking, not coding.

You could put the most powerful machine on every desk. But if it requires 40 hours of training to use it, you've already lost.

The winner isn't the breakthrough that's most technically impressive.

It's the one that requires the least effort to understand.

The smartest thing Larry Ellison did wasn't building better software.

It was choosing the right enemy.

When Oracle was fighting Informix and Caiase for market share, nobody cared.

So Ellison did something counterintuitive:

He stopped fighting his actual competitors.

Instead, he picked a fight with Microsoft and IBM.

"We pick our enemies very carefully. It helps us focus... If you're a fighter, the only way up is through the top fighters in your division. So, we picked fights with Microsoft and IBM because they're the ones we had to beat to reach the top."

The positioning was genius.

When you're positioning Oracle against smaller database companies, you're fighting for scraps in a niche market.

When you position Oracle against Microsoft? Suddenly you're a heavyweight.

The media came. Fortune magazine put him on the cover. "Software's other billionaire."

Customers started thinking differently:

"Oracle is in the ring with Microsoft. They must be serious. They're not going anywhere. They're a survivor."

Caiase and Informix couldn't say the same thing.

They weren't fighting anyone. They were just... there.

Ellison understood something most competitors miss:

"Your position in the market isn't determined by who you actually beat. It's determined by who you're willing to fight."

The original iPod launched at $399, worked only with Macs, and got savaged by critics.

"Way overpriced." "Too limited." One famous headline called it the "Wheel of Fortune"... And not as a compliment.

Tony Fadell shipped it anyway.

Then he shipped 17 more versions.

Windows compatibility. The Mini. The Nano. The price cuts.

Each one closing the gap between what they'd announced and what they'd actually imagined.

By the time the iPod peaked, it had sold 400 million units and quietly become the foundation for the iPhone.

Most people remember the iPod as a huge win for Apple but in reality the first version was expensive, Mac-only, and widely mocked.

The product that changed music forever needed several generations to become itself.

That's the thing nobody tells you about great products.

"The launch isn't the achievement. The launch is the permission to keep going."

"It's better to have 100 people that love you than a million people that just sort of like you."

Brian Chesky considers this to be the best advice he's ever received.

In 2009, Chesky felt stuck because Airbnb only had a handful of users.

The gap between where he was and where he wanted to be felt uncrossable.

"How the hell am I gonna get a million people to use this if I can't even get my mom or my sister to use it?"

Paul Graham advised him to narrow his focus to 100 users.

"Your first 100 users should feel that signing up with you was one of the best choices they ever made. And you in turn should be racking your brains to think of new ways to delight them."

Graham calls this "doing things that don't scale."

And Chesky and his co-founders took this about as far as anyone ever has.

They noticed early on that Airbnb listings with bad photos weren't getting booked. So they flew to New York with a camera and went door to door photographing their hosts' apartments themselves. While they were there, they also coached their hosts on writing better listing descriptions, and handled support calls in person.

Chesky even took it one step further.

He spent nearly a year living in Airbnbs around San Francisco to be closer to his users and solve their problems.

This manic devotion echoes what Ben Silbermann did at Pinterest.

In the early days, Silbermann personally emailed his first several thousand users, put his phone number in the support replies, and spent afternoons in Palo Alto coffee shops watching strangers try his app.

The Collison brothers did their own version of this at Stripe.

In 2011, when prospective customer showed interest, the Collisons would install the Stripe API on their site right there in the meeting. Most signups never finished the integration. So doing the install themselves made sure they didn't lose users.

Graham famously nicknamed this personal support the "Collison installation."

No large company can give their users this level of care at scale.

But that's why it works.

Users who love your product stick around and spread the word for you.

Airbnb is proof.

As Chesky tells it: "I once asked an early host how many people she'd told about Airbnb. She said a thousand. She'd been telling people every day for three years."

Chesky never did figure out how to get a million people to use Airbnb.

His first 100 users did it for him.

One of the more unusual things Steve Jobs did when building the Mac was refuse to do any market research.

"We didn't build the Mac for anybody else," he said. "We built it for ourselves. We were the group of people who were going to judge whether it was great or not."

This sounds reckless, and in most situations it would be.

But Jobs was very intentional about this.

"We weren't going to go out and do market research. We just wanted to build the best thing we could build."

The trouble with building what customers say they want is that customers don't actually know.

They can tell you what's wrong with the product in front of them. But they can't describe something they've never seen. If you ask them what they want, you'll get a better version of what already exists… You won't get the Mac.

As Henry Ford famously said:

"If I had asked people what they wanted, they would have said faster horses."

In practice, this meant that every feature, every decision, and every pixel had to pass through the judgment of whoever was sitting in the room.

The test was always: "Would we use it?"

If the answer was no, the feature didn't ship.

But this sounds easier than it is.

It only works if the people in the room have taste. And if they trust their taste enough to reject things a committee might approve.

Research can tell you what people know they want. But the most interesting products are the ones nobody knew they wanted, because nobody had imagined them yet.

You have to imagine them first.

And the only way to know if you've imagined something good is to ask whether you'd use it.

When Jobs built the Mac, customers turned out to want it.

But the market didn't get a vote until after the product existed.

Jeff Bezos once described himself as Amazon's Chief Slowdown Officer.

"I often found myself in the position of being the chief slowdown officer... I would say okay, I can think of three more ways to analyze that."

Bezos slowed things down because he treated every decision as if they were equally important.

This is the default for most executives.

You want to be sure about a decision before committing.

But what Bezos eventually realized is that this rationale gets you into trouble for one large category of decisions.

Some decisions can be reversed. Others can't.

He called them Two-Way Doors vs One-Way Doors:

"If you make the wrong decision, if it's a Two-Way Door decision, you walk out the door, and you spend a little time there. If it turns out to be the wrong decision, you can come back in and pick another door."

The math is pretty easy to follow:

A wrong Two-Way Door decision costs you some time and iteration, but you can always come back from it.

A wrong One-Way Door decision can cost you the company. It's irreversible.

When the cost of the decision making process doesn't match the cost of a wrong decision, you overpay in both directions. Reversible decisions get treated with more care than they need, and irreversible decisions sometimes get less care than they deserve.

Bezos's fix was to push two-way door decisions down to the people closest to the problem:

"Two-way door decisions should mostly be made by single individuals or by very small teams deep in the organization."

And one-way door decisions would get more time and attention from the execs at the top.

This sounds obvious in retrospect, but what it does is match the cost of a decision to the cost of getting it wrong.
